questions.q: What happens if you change a signed message without changing anything else, in the live demo?
options: Verification fails — the signature was created for the exact original message
The signature automatically updates to match
Nothing changes, verification still passes
The private key gets deleted
questions.explain: A signature is tied to the exact message it signed — altering the message afterward breaks verification, exactly as intended.

options: The first transaction in a block, created by the miner, with no inputs — this is how new coins enter circulation
A transaction that can only happen on the Coinbase exchange
The very last transaction recorded in a block
A transaction that transfers ownership of the entire blockchain
questions.explain: Unlike every other transaction, a Coinbase transaction has no inputs — it's how the miner is rewarded and how new coins actually get minted.

questions.q: What does the "previous hash" field inside a block actually do?
options: Stores the hash of the prior block, forming the literal chain in "blockchain"
Stores the miner's private key
Records how many transactions are in the block
Has no real function — it's just decorative
questions.explain: Every block (except the first) includes the previous block's hash — that link is what actually makes it a chain.

questions.q: What happens if you change a transaction inside a block and then re-mine it?
options: The block's hash changes completely, breaking the link to every block after it
Nothing changes — the hash stays exactly the same
Only the transaction amount changes, not the hash
The entire blockchain automatically deletes itself
questions.explain: Because the hash is calculated from the block's actual contents, changing any transaction inside it produces a completely different hash — visible tampering, immediately.

questions.q: What real mechanism lets anyone verify that a specific person actually sent a transaction?
options: The sender signs the transaction with their private key; anyone can verify it using the sender's public key
The receiver has to personally call the sender to confirm
Transactions can't actually be verified at all
A bank manually approves each transaction
questions.explain: This is the same signing/verifying mechanism from Chapter 2, now applied directly to a real transaction — sign with private key, verify with public key.
